title: Vishvamitra and the forbidden food
hookLine: in a famine, a great sage creeps into a hut at night to steal a piece of dog meat, and gets caught
carry: apaddharma: dharma bends to save a life
tomorrow: a hunter shelters under a pigeon's tree. what is a guest owed?

cards: Yudhishthira asks a hard question. What happens to dharma when everything falls apart? When there's war, famine, collapse, and the normal rules can't be kept?
Bhishma's answer is a whole section called Apaddharma, dharma in times of distress. To explain it, he tells a story that's uncomfortable on purpose. A great sage, Vishvamitra, is starving.
The rains have failed for a long time. The fields are dust, the villages empty, and people eat whatever they can find. One night, half dead, Vishvamitra slips into a poor hamlet looking for food.

teach.b: In one hut he sees the haunch of a dog hanging. By the rules of his world, it's deeply forbidden food for a man like him. He decides to take it anyway.
But the man who lives there wakes and catches him, and what follows isn't a fight. It's a debate.

teach.h: THE HOUSEHOLDER ARGUES FOR THE RULES
teach.b: The householder, a man the society of that time placed at the bottom, argues for the rules. You're a sage, he says. You know dharma.
Don't do this. Vishvamitra argues back.
Staying alive comes first, because only the living can practice dharma at all. When I'm through this, I'll make amends with austerity. A dead sage helps no one.
The householder isn't fully convinced, but Vishvamitra takes the meat, and even now, the story says, he means to offer it to the gods before he eats. Then the god Indra sends rain.
The great sage steals; the man at the bottom defends dharma; the story leaves the discomfort in place. Two Hindu teachings sit inside it.

teach.h: DHARMA BENDS TO SAVE A LIFE
teach.b: Apaddharma: in real distress, dharma bends to protect life. And prayashchitta: the amends you make afterward, which is why Vishvamitra speaks of austerity even with the meat in his hand.
But Bhishma warns this is for real distress, not convenience. A king who calls every inconvenience a famine has missed the lesson. You can still see this in Hindu homes.
Many teachers say the sick and the very old may eat on a fast day, or keep a lighter fast with fruit or milk. The fast serves life. It was never meant to cost one.

how: Hindu teachers and writers on dharma discuss Apaddharma, the conduct allowed in real distress, and the story of Vishvamitra and the dog meat is told as a hard example of it.

dharma for times of disaster, when rules can't hold
the penance a sage does after breaking a vow

games.q: dharma in distress — tap the pairs.
p: steals the dog meat to live

s: the householder helped Vishvamitra steal the meat
he caught him and argued that a sage should not do it.
Vishvamitra argued that only the living can practice dharma
survival first, he said, then amends through austerity.
Vishvamitra planned to make amends afterward
he spoke of austerity to repair what he broke; Hindu teaching calls such amends prayashchitta.

games.q: a friend says: 'if dharma can bend in a famine, i can skip my promises whenever i'm busy.' by Bhishma's teaching, what's the answer?
o: no: it bends only in real distress, to protect life, and you make amends after.
no: dharma never bends, not even in a famine.
games.why: apaddharma is for real distress, not convenience, and it comes with prayashchitta, the amends afterward. busy isn't a famine.

practice: Let your breath settle and bring to mind a time you bent one of your own rules because things were falling apart.
Breathe in and remember what was at stake; breathe out and ask honestly, without judging yourself, whether it was a real emergency or just convenience, and whether anything still needs repairing.
If you pray, you can bring it into your prayer.
